name: BeeCrypt
baseline: Java multiprecision-integer modular exponentiation (JVM 1.2.2 to 1.4.0; the file says only 'Java', presumably java.math.BigInteger)
workload: Modular exponentiation (1024-bit base ^ 1024-bit exponent mod 1024-bit modulus), 100 repetitions, wall time in seconds (less is better), BeeCrypt 2.0 to 2.2 (C with assembler) versus several Java VMs on 1999 to 2002 era machines.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS file text: 'as of version 1.0.1 BeeCrypt now beats Java on every platform, including UltraSparc. Depending on the version of Java, BeeCrypt is from twice to four times faster.' Same-machine rows: Pentium III 600 / Windows 2000 / 256 MB: BeeCrypt 2.1.0 (Visual C 6.0) 4.3 sec vs Java 1.4.0 Sun Server VM 10.2 sec (~2.4x, derived from page data) and Sun Client VM 19.7 sec (~4.6x, derived from page data); Pentium III 450 / Solaris 8 / 128 MB: BeeCrypt 2.0.0 (gcc-2.95.2) 5.9 sec vs Java 1.3 Sun Server VM 17.1 sec (~2.9x, derived from page data); UltraSparc I 143 / Solaris 8 / 128 MB: BeeCrypt 2.0.0 (Forte C++ 6.1, 64-bit) 40.7 sec vs Java 1.3.1 Sun Server VM 83.4 sec (~2.0x, derived from page data). The file also says 'both on Solaris and Linux, beecrypt is least 5 times faster for this operation than a commercial product we at one time considered using' (product not named).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler named per row (Visual C 6.0, gcc-2.95.2, gcc-2.95.3, Forte C++ 6.1); optimization flags not stated in this revision; benchmark program is tests/benchme.c in the same CVS tree
hardware: Per row, 1999 to 2002 era: Pentium III 450/600/800/1000, Athlon 1000/1200, Pentium 4M 1700, Alpha EV6.7 667, UltraSparc I 143 and II 450/400, PowerPC 604/G3/7450, Itanium, StrongARM; Java rows were measured on a different set of machines, only a few coincide with BeeCrypt rows
stars_or_usage: SourceForge project, 161 downloads in the latest tracked week, 2 reviews (5.0 of 5); CVS only, no star count
tradeoffs: LGPL copyleft. C library with assembler routines for several CPUs (NEWS mentions x86 and PowerPC; gas and masm directories in the tree) plus C++ and Java glue. Primitive set in the CVS tree is older: MD5, SHA-1/2, RIPEMD, Blowfish, AES in ECB/CBC, RSA, DSA, ElGamal, Diffie-Hellman; no GCM, ChaCha20, Poly1305 or Curve25519 sources in the file listing. Project website beecrypt.sourceforge.net is a placeholder page; source lives at sourceforge.net/projects/beecrypt.
caveats: The only numeric comparison reachable is against Java on 1999 to 2003 era hardware and JVMs (the table was removed from BENCHMARKS in revision 1.18, 2003-05-20; the newest revision 1.35 holds only BeeCrypt-alone numbers, e.g. modular exponentiation score 64747 on a Core i7-2600). It says nothing about OpenSSL, libsodium or BoringSSL, so it is far off the usual incumbents and baseline_in_list is false. Java and BeeCrypt rows are mostly on different machines; the ratios quoted above use rows where machine and OS match as closely as the file allows. The 5x-over-a-commercial-product remark names no product. An independent 2008 panthema.net speedtest (OpenSSL vs BeeCrypt vs Crypto++ vs Botan) exists but the host is EGRESS_BLOCKED here and search summaries gave conflicting AES numbers (BeeCrypt ahead of OpenSSL on one distro, about half its speed on another), so none of it is used. The benchmark page URL is a CVS snapshot zip; the data is in beecrypt/beecrypt/BENCHMARKS,v (revision 1.17 of 2003-01-28 and earlier). Unmaintained since 2015.

name: CRC++
workload: README comparison table: wall time in milliseconds for 100 million iterations of a CRC computation on an x64 and an x86 build, against boost, pycrc and mhash; input size, CRC variant and table-versus-bitwise mode are not stated.
claimed_speedup: x64: CRC++ 2050 ms vs boost 2250 ms (~1.10x faster, derived from page data), pycrc 2050 ms (tie), mhash 2250 ms (~1.10x, derived). x86: CRC++ 2200 ms vs boost 2000 ms (boost ~1.10x faster, derived), pycrc 2240 ms, mhash 2400 ms. README wording: 'one of the fastest and most memory efficient generic CRC implementation available'.
tradeoffs: Single header (inc/CRC.h), C++03 or C++11, any CRC width including odd ones, 40+ built-in CRC definitions, bit-by-bit or lookup-table modes, optional branchless bitwise mode, multipart CRCs. The README describes only bitwise and table-driven code; no SIMD or hardware CRC32 path is mentioned.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler, flags, input size or CRC polynomial, and no benchmark code in the repo (test/src/main.cpp holds unit tests only; no timing code found), so it cannot be reproduced. The win is about 10% on x64 over boost and mhash, a tie with pycrc, and a loss to boost on x86. Baselines are generic CRC libraries; SIMD and hardware-instruction CRC32 libraries (zlib, libdeflate, crc32fast, ISA-L style PCLMUL code) are not compared and are typically much faster on large buffers.

name: Rain (Rainbow hash)
baseline: HighwayHash-128 and FarmHash-128.CM (128-bit hashes in the SMHasher3 results table); the repo names no baseline itself
workload: SMHasher3 Speed test as published in the SMHasher3 results README: average cycles/hash over 1-31-byte keys and bulk bytes/cycle at 262144-byte keys, Rainbow 128-bit and 256-bit v3.7.1 against the other hashes that pass all tests. Results page does not name the CPU (harness prints '@ 3.5 ghz').
claimed_speedup: Claim only (README): 'Rainbow is the fastest 128-bit hash, and the fastest 256-bit hash (non-crypto)'; README table gives Rainbow 3-6 GiB/s with no baseline. SMHasher3 results page data: rainbow-128 62.06 cycles on 1-31 byte keys vs HighwayHash-128 99.09 (~1.6x faster, derived from page data), FarmHash-128.CM.seed1 69.61 (~1.1x), MeowHash 61.51 (tie); rainbow-256 103.65 vs HighwayHash-256 154.48 (~1.5x) and PearsonBlock-256 168.68. Not faster elsewhere: rainbow-128 is slower than a5hash-128 (30.27) and MuseAir-128 (30.97) on short keys, and bulk is 1.27 bytes/cycle (4.14 GiB/s at the assumed 3.5 GHz) vs HighwayHash-128 2.87, a5hash-128 6.92, MuseAir-128 7.15 and MeowHash 12.43; rainbow-256 bulk 1.28 vs HighwayHash-256 2.88 and RH512 2.50.
tradeoffs: Rainbow is a roughly 140-line multiply/rotate hash with scalable 64, 128 or 256-bit output that passes all 250 SMHasher3 tests (64-bit variant claimed), but its bulk speed is low (about 1.3 bytes/cycle). The repo also ships Rainstorm, a slower experimental crypto-style hash whose v4 README says an external review found a practical collision for a two-message-round reduction; it is unvetted. WASM port is 4x to 23x slower than the C++ build (README benchmark).
caveats: The README headline claim (fastest 128-bit and 256-bit non-crypto hash) is not supported by the SMHasher3 results page it links: several passing 128-bit hashes (a5hash-128, MuseAir-128, MeowHash) are faster in bulk and on short keys, and at 256 bits HighwayHash-256 and CityHashCrc-256 (which fails some tests) are faster in bulk. The only wins found are narrow (short-key latency against HighwayHash and FarmHash). SMHasher3 results list the CPU nowhere and the table is the maintainer's single run; Rain's README credits SMHasher3's maintainer for improvements to the code, so the suite is not fully arm's length. The claim may predate v3.7.1 (not checked). The repo's own results/smhasher3/rainbow-256-v3.7.1.txt came back as an empty file through raw.githubusercontent.com and was not used. The assigned URL github.com/DOSAYGO-Research/rain resolves to DOSAYGO-STUDIO/rain.
